questions.q: $\text{A} + \text{B} = \text{C} + \text{D}$. If initially the concentration of $\text{A}\text{a}\text{n}\text{d}\text{B}$ are both equal but at equilibrium, concentration of $\text{D}$ will be twice of that of $\text{A}$, then what will be the equilibrium constant of reaction?

Let the initial concentration be 'a'

$\begin{cases} & \text{A} & + & \text{B} & \to & \text{C} & + & \text{D} \\ \text{Initial} & \text{a} & & \text{a} & & 0 & & 0 \\ \text{at equilibrium} & \text{a} - \text{x} & & \text{a} - \text{x} & & x & & x\end{cases}$

$\begin{array}{ll}\text{given}\text{x} = 2\left(\text{a} - \text{x}\right) = 2\text{a} - 2\text{x} \\ \text{3x} = \left(\text{2a}\right) \\ \text{x} = \dfrac{2}{3} \text{a}\end{array}$

at eq. $\begin{cases}⇒ & \dfrac{\text{a}}{3} & \dfrac{\text{a}}{3} & \dfrac{2 \text{a}}{3} & \dfrac{2 \text{a}}{3}\end{cases}$

${K}_{eq} = \dfrac{\left[\text{C}\right] \left[\text{D}\right]}{\left[\text{A}\right] \left[\text{B}\right]} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{2 \text{a}}{3}\right) \left(\dfrac{\text{2a}}{3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{\text{a}}{3}\right) \left(\dfrac{\text{a}}{3}\right)} = 4$

questions.q:
Consider the following reaction equilibrium

${N}_{2}\left(g\right) + 3{H}_{2} ( g ) ⇌ 2N{H}_{3} ( g )$

Initially, 1 mole of ${N}_{2}$ and 3 moles of ${H}_{2}$ are taken in a 2 L flask. At equilibrium state if, the number of moles of ${N}_{2}$is 0.6, what is the total number of moles of all gases present in the flask?
questions.solution:
Number of moles of ${\text{N}}_{2} = 0.6 = 1 - \text{x}$

$∴$ $\text{x} = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4$

So, $3 - 3\text{x} = 3 - 3 \times 0.4 = 1.8$,

and $2\text{x} = 2 \times 0.4 = 0.8$

Therefore, the total number of moles at equilibrium.

$= \left(1 - \text{x}\right) + \left(3 - 3\text{x}\right) + 2\text{x}$

$= 0.6 + 1.8 + 0.8$

$= 3.2$ mol

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which can be explained as applications of Le Chatelier's principle?
options: Transport of oxygen by haemoglobin in blood
Removal of $C{O}_{2}$ from tissues by blood
Tooth decay due to use of sweet substances
questions.solution:
(i) The haemoglobin of RBC combines with oxygen in lungs following the equilibrium,
${H}_{b} ( s ) + {O}_{2} ( g ) ⇌ {H}_{b}{O}_{2} ( s )$
When these are at lungs, the partial pressure of ${O}_{2}$ being appreciable show forward reaction, however when they pass to tissues, the partial pressure of ${O}_{2}$ decreases to favour backward reaction releasing ${O}_{2}$.
(ii) Removal of $C{O}_{2}$ from blood is based on the equilibrium,
$C{O}_{2} ( g ) + {H}_{2}O ( l ) ⇌ H^{+} ( aq ) + HC{O}_{3}^{-} ( aq )$
In tissues $C{O}_{2}$ gets dissolved in ${H}_{2}O$ due to high pressure whereas in lungs, the $C{O}_{2}$ is released out because of low pressure of $C{O}_{2}$.
(iii) Tooth enamel substance (Hydroxyapatite) $C{a}_{5} ( P{O}_{4}{)}_{3}OH$ shows the following equilibrium,
${\text{Ca}_{5} {{\text{(PO}_{4} \text{)}_{3} \text{OH}\overset{\text{Demineralization}}{⇌} {\text{5Ca}^{\text{2+}} ( \text{aq} ) \text{+}{\text{3PO}_{4}^{\text{3} -} ( \text{aq} ) \text{+}{\text{OH}^{−} ( \text{aq} )$
The use of sweet material or fermentation produces $H^{+}$. Which combines with $\overset{-}{O}H$ to favour demineralisation of enamel causing tooth decay.
